scores.Rationale: The proposal addresses a significant and underexplored issue in physical therapy—differential diagnosis of Lyme disease—highlighting an important gap in both education and clinical practice. The dual-aim design to assess curricular trends and clinical competencies positions the study to make meaningful contributions for educational reform and patient care improvement.

The methodological plan is well-structured with clear inclusion criteria, validated survey instruments, and defined recruitment strategies including in-person and online data collection. While the study design is feasible and appropriate for the aims, there is some uncertainty regarding the sufficiency of sample size for generalizability and managing possible recruitment challenges.

The PI and co-investigators have strong relevant expertise in physical therapy education, survey design, and content knowledge of Lyme disease. The inclusion of a physician assistant faculty adds complementary expertise, strengthening interdisciplinary insight and fit to the project.

The study aligns well with external funder priorities such as the ILADEF and has a clear pathway to future interventional studies. The focus on education and clinical practice improvement increases its competitiveness for funding targeting health professions education and tick-borne diseases.

The budget is modest, well-justified, and primarily directed towards participant incentives, travel, and research assistant support to ensure data collection and management. The allocation supports the study aims effectively without excess.

The application is generally clear and well-organized with logical flow across sections. Some minor typographical errors and formatting issues slightly hinder readability but do not obscure the content or aims.
